heuristics.rule: 2-year cohabitation threshold for statutory property-division rights
heuristics.condition: When an unmarried couple in British Columbia has lived together in a marriage-like relationship for at least two years
heuristics.action: The same property-division rights that apply to married couples under BC's Family Law Act apply to the unmarried couple
heuristics.because: BC's Family Law Act explicitly extends married-couple property-division rights to unmarried couples who meet the 2-year threshold; below two years, no statutory property-division right exists by default
heuristics.regulatory_basis: BC Family Law Act — 2-year marriage-like relationship threshold

heuristics.rule: Pre-relationship property stays separate; property acquired during the relationship is shared
heuristics.condition: When the 2-year threshold is met and the couple separates
heuristics.action: Property brought into the relationship by either partner remains that partner's separate property; property acquired together during the relationship is divided
heuristics.because: BC's Family Law Act specifies that common-law partners 'will generally share any property they acquire during the course of their relationship — but not property brought into the relationship'
heuristics.regulatory_basis: BC Family Law Act — family property definition for common-law couples

heuristics.rule: Written agreement can opt out of default statutory property-division rules
heuristics.condition: When an unmarried couple in BC does not want the Family Law Act's default property-division rules to apply
heuristics.action: The couple must execute a written agreement contracting out of the statutory default rules
heuristics.because: BC's Family Law Act permits couples to contract out entirely via a written agreement; without such an agreement, the statutory defaults apply automatically once the 2-year threshold is met
heuristics.regulatory_basis: BC Family Law Act — opt-out via written agreement

heuristics.rule: Province is a required diagnostic fact for any Canadian unmarried couple considering separation and property division
heuristics.condition: When a Canadian user who is unmarried asks what happens to shared property if they leave a relationship
heuristics.action: Identify the province before answering; BC and Ontario have materially different rules and a generic 'Canada' answer is not valid
heuristics.because: BC grants automatic property-division rights after 2 years of cohabitation; Ontario does not grant automatic property division to common-law couples regardless of duration — province determines whether statutory rights exist at all
heuristics.regulatory_basis: BC Family Law Act vs. Ontario family law framework (province-variance principle)

decision_factors.factor: Duration of cohabitation in a marriage-like relationship
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Determines whether statutory property-division rights under BC's Family Law Act are triggered at all; the threshold is exactly 2 years
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Calculate continuous time living together in a marriage-like relationship; if at least 2 years, statutory rights apply; if under 2 years, no default statutory property-division right exists

decision_factors.factor: Whether a written opt-out agreement exists
decision_factors.why_it_matters: A written agreement can entirely displace the statutory default property-division rules, meaning the Family Law Act's protections may not apply even if the 2-year threshold is met
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Determine whether the couple executed a written agreement contracting out of the Family Law Act's default property-division rules prior to or during the relationship

decision_factors.factor: Timing of asset acquisition — before vs. during the relationship
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Pre-relationship assets remain separate and are not subject to division; only assets acquired during the relationship are generally shared
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify the date each asset was acquired relative to the start of the marriage-like relationship; assets acquired before the relationship began are excluded from division

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Property-division rights for unmarried couples vary dramatically by province; BC grants automatic rights after 2 years, while Ontario does not grant automatic property division to common-law couples regardless of duration
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Confirm which Canadian province the couple resides in before applying any property-division analysis; a generic 'Canada' framework is insufficient

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Cohabiting in BC without a written opt-out agreement past the 2-year mark
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Once the 2-year threshold is crossed, the statutory property-division rules of BC's Family Law Act apply automatically and with the same force as they do for married couples — there is no opt-out after the fact without a written agreement executed before or during the relationship
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Unmarried partners who assume common-law cohabitation carries no formal property consequences and have not documented their intentions in a written agreement

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Relying on a generic 'Canadian common-law' understanding of property rights
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: A user in BC has near-equivalent property rights to a married person after 2 years, while a user in Ontario has no automatic statutory property-division right regardless of how long they cohabited — applying the wrong provincial framework produces materially incorrect conclusions about what a departing partner is entitled to
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Canadian users in any province other than the one whose rules they are applying, particularly those moving between BC and Ontario or unaware of provincial variance

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Leaving a relationship before the 2-year cohabitation threshold in BC
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Departing before 2 years of marriage-like cohabitation eliminates any statutory property-division claim under BC's Family Law Act; there is no default right to share property acquired during the relationship below that threshold
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Partners who contributed financially or materially to a relationship of less than 2 years duration in BC and expect a share of jointly accumulated assets

failure_patterns.pattern: Claiming statutory property-division rights in BC after less than 2 years of marriage-like cohabitation
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: BC's Family Law Act requires at least 2 years of living together in a marriage-like relationship before property-division rights are triggered; below this threshold no statutory right exists by default
failure_patterns.consequence: No statutory property-division right; claim fails under the Family Law Act
warning_signs: No written agreement establishing alternative property arrangements exists

failure_patterns.pattern: Attempting to claim a share of a partner's pre-relationship assets at separation
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: BC's Family Law Act explicitly excludes property brought into the relationship from the pool of family property subject to division; only assets acquired during the relationship are generally shared
failure_patterns.consequence: Claim to pre-relationship assets fails; those assets remain the separate property of the partner who brought them into the relationship
warning_signs: Asset was owned by one partner before the relationship began
No written agreement altering the default pre-relationship exclusion

failure_patterns.pattern: Applying Ontario common-law property rules to a BC couple or vice versa
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Province-specific rules are materially different; BC grants automatic property-division rights after 2 years, Ontario does not grant automatic rights regardless of duration — conflating them produces incorrect outcomes
failure_patterns.consequence: Materially incorrect assessment of property entitlements, potentially causing a party to forgo or overclaim rights they do or do not have
warning_signs: User or advisor refers to 'Canadian common-law rules' without specifying province
Analysis does not confirm province before applying property-division framework

diagnostic_questions.question: In which Canadian province does the couple reside or did they reside during the relationship?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Which provincial property-division framework applies; BC and Ontario have materially different rules for unmarried couples and province is a threshold diagnostic fact
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If BC: proceed to assess 2-year cohabitation threshold and written opt-out agreement
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If not BC: apply the relevant provincial framework; do not apply BC Family Law Act rules

diagnostic_questions.question: Have the partners lived together in a marriage-like relationship for at least 2 years?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the 2-year threshold under BC's Family Law Act is met, which is the gateway condition for any statutory property-division right to exist
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Statutory property-division rights under BC's Family Law Act apply unless a written opt-out agreement exists
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: No statutory property-division right exists by default under BC's Family Law Act; assess whether any written agreement creates alternative rights

diagnostic_questions.question: Did the couple execute a written agreement contracting out of BC's Family Law Act default property-division rules?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the statutory defaults have been displaced by private agreement, which entirely removes the Family Law Act's automatic property-division framework
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: The written agreement governs property division; the Family Law Act defaults do not apply
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: The Family Law Act's default property-division rules apply automatically if the 2-year threshold is met

diagnostic_questions.question: Was the asset in question acquired before or during the relationship?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the asset falls within the 'family property' pool subject to division or is excluded as pre-relationship property
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If acquired during the relationship: asset is generally subject to division under BC's Family Law Act
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If brought into the relationship: asset is excluded from division and remains the separate property of the partner who owned it pre-relationship

industry_realities.common_belief: Common-law couples in Canada do not have the same property rights as married couples
industry_realities.actual_reality: In British Columbia specifically, unmarried couples who have lived together in a marriage-like relationship for at least 2 years have essentially the same statutory property-division rights as married couples under BC's Family Law Act; this is not true in Ontario, where no automatic property-division right exists for common-law couples regardless of duration
industry_realities.implication: A BC common-law partner past the 2-year mark must be advised using the same property-division framework as a married person; assuming no rights exist is factually incorrect under BC law

industry_realities.common_belief: Property-division rules for common-law couples are the same across Canada
industry_realities.actual_reality: Province determines the applicable rules entirely; BC grants automatic property-division rights after 2 years of marriage-like cohabitation, while Ontario grants no automatic statutory property division to common-law couples regardless of how long they lived together
industry_realities.implication: Any advisor or tool answering a Canadian unmarried person's question about property division on separation must obtain the province before applying any framework; a generic 'Canada' answer is not valid

industry_realities.common_belief: Before 2013, unmarried BC couples had the same property rights they have today
industry_realities.actual_reality: Before 2013, unmarried couples in BC had no statutory right to court-ordered property division at all; the current rights were created by legislative reform reflecting the increasing prevalence of common-law families
industry_realities.implication: Advice or case outcomes from before 2013 in BC are not reliable precedent for current statutory rights; the legal landscape changed materially with the Family Law Act reform

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Answering a Canadian unmarried person's property question on separation
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Applies a generic 'Canadian common-law' framework or assumes common-law couples have no property rights, without asking for province
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Identifies province as the threshold diagnostic fact before any analysis; applies BC Family Law Act framework (2-year threshold, family property definition, written opt-out) for BC residents, and separately identifies that Ontario has no automatic property division for common-law couples
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Applying the wrong provincial framework produces materially incorrect conclusions about whether a statutory property-division right exists at all and what assets are in scope

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Assessing whether a BC common-law partner has property rights
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Assumes that because the couple is unmarried, property rights are minimal or non-existent regardless of how long they lived together
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Checks the 2-year cohabitation threshold first; if met, applies the same property-division analysis as for a married couple under BC's Family Law Act, then checks for a written opt-out agreement that could displace the statutory defaults
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: A BC common-law partner past 2 years who is not informed of their statutory rights may forfeit entitlements to assets accumulated during the relationship that the Family Law Act would automatically protect

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Advising on the effect of a written cohabitation agreement in BC
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Treats a cohabitation agreement as a best-practice nicety but assumes the statutory defaults still apply
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Recognizes that a written agreement can entirely contract out of BC's Family Law Act default property-division rules, meaning the statutory framework is fully displaced if such an agreement exists — the agreement, not the Act, governs the outcome
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Failing to check for a written opt-out agreement before applying the Family Law Act defaults produces incorrect property-division analysis for couples who have contracted out
